paragraphs: “N—not particularly,” Kolya answered offhandedly. “What ruined my reputation here more than anything was that cursed goose,” he said, turning to Ilusha again. He put on an unconcerned air while he talked, but he still couldn’t keep himself in hand, and he kept missing the note he was trying to hold.
“Oh! I heard about the goose!” Ilusha laughed, beaming all over. “They told me, but I didn’t get it. Did they really haul you up before a court?”

“It was the stupidest, most trivial business. They made a mountain out of a molehill, the way they always do,” Kolya began carelessly. “One day I was walking across the market-place, just when they’d driven in the geese. I stopped to look at them. Suddenly a fellow who’s an errand-boy at Plotnikov’s now looked at me and said, ‘What are you staring at the geese for?’ I looked him over. He was a dull, moon-faced fellow of twenty. I’m always on the side of the peasants, you know. I like talking to them.... We’ve fallen behind the peasants—that’s an axiom. I think you’re laughing, Karamazov?”
“No, heaven forbid, I’m listening,” said Alyosha, looking perfectly good-natured, and the touchy Kolya was reassured at once.

“My theory, Karamazov, is clear and simple,” he hurried on again, looking pleased. “I believe in the people, and I’m always glad to give them their due, but I’m not for spoiling them. That’s a _sine qua non_ ... But I was telling you about the goose. So I turned to the fool and said, ‘I’m wondering what that goose is thinking about.’ He gave me a quite blank look. ‘And what is it thinking about?’ he asked. ‘See that cart full of oats?’ I said. ‘The oats are spilling out of the sack, and the goose has put its neck right under the wheel to gobble them up—see?’ ‘I see that fine,’ he said. ‘Well,’ I said, ‘if the cart rolled forward a bit, would it break the goose’s neck or not?’ ‘Sure to break it,’ he said, and grinned from ear to ear, delighted. ‘Come on, then,’ I said, ‘let’s try it.’ ‘Let’s,’ he said. It didn’t take long to set up. He slipped over to the horse’s bridle without being noticed, and I stood off to one side to steer the goose. The owner wasn’t watching, he was busy talking to somebody, so I hardly had to do a thing: the goose stuck its head in after the oats all by itself, under the cart, right under the wheel. I winked at the lad, he gave the bridle a tug, and crack! The goose’s neck was snapped in half. And, just my luck, every peasant there saw us at that very moment and started a row at once. ‘You did that on purpose!’ ‘No, not on purpose.’ ‘Yes, you did, on purpose!’ Then they shouted, ‘Take him to the justice of the peace!’ They dragged me along too. ‘You were in it too,’ they said, ‘you helped, the whole market knows you!’ And for some reason the whole market really does know me,” Kolya added conceitedly. “We all trooped off to the justice’s, and they brought the goose along as well. The fellow was in a great funk and crying, simply blubbering like a woman. And the farmer kept shouting that at this rate you could kill any number of geese. Well, of course, there were witnesses. The justice settled it in a minute: the farmer was to get a rouble for the goose, and the fellow could keep the goose. And he was warned not to try such pranks again. And the fellow went on blubbering like a woman. ‘It wasn’t me,’ he said, ‘he put me up to it,’ and he pointed at me. I replied with perfect calm that I hadn’t put him up to anything, I’d merely stated a general proposition, speaking hypothetically. The justice smiled, and immediately was annoyed with himself for smiling. ‘I’ll report you to your masters,’ he said, ‘so that in future you’ll stop wasting your time on general propositions and sit at your books learning your lessons instead.’ He didn’t report me to the masters, that was a joke, but the story got around and reached their ears. They’ve got long ears, you know! The classics master, Kolbasnikov, was especially scandalized, but Dardanelov got me off again. Kolbasnikov is savage with everybody now, like a green ass. Did you know, Ilusha, he’s just married, and got a dowry of a thousand roubles, and his bride is a regular fright of the first rank and the last degree. The third-class boys wrote an epigram about it:
Astounding news has reached the class, Kolbasnikov has been an ass.
And so on, awfully funny, I’ll bring it to you later. I’ve nothing against Dardanelov. He’s a learned man, no doubt about it. I respect men like that, and not because he stood up for me.”
“But you caught him out about the founders of Troy!” Smurov put in suddenly, plainly proud of Krassotkin at such a moment. The story of the goose had pleased him especially.
“Did you really catch him out?” the captain asked, flatteringly. “On who founded Troy? We heard about that. Ilusha told me at the time.”
“He knows everything, father, he knows more than any of us!” put in Ilusha. “He only acts like that, but really he’s top in every subject....”
Ilusha looked at Kolya with boundless happiness.

“Oh, all that about Troy is nonsense, a trifle. I consider it an unimportant question,” said Kolya, with haughty humility. By now he had fully regained his dignity, though he was still a little uneasy. He knew he was very worked up, and that he had told the story of the goose, for one thing, with too little restraint, while Alyosha had looked serious and hadn’t said a word the whole time. And little by little the vain boy began to be gnawed by the fear that Alyosha was silent because he despised him, and thought he was showing off. If he dared to think anything like that, Kolya would—
“I regard the question as quite trivial,” he snapped again, proudly.

“And I know who founded Troy,” said a boy who hadn’t spoken before, suddenly, to everyone’s surprise. He had sat silent and seemed shy. He was a pretty boy of about eleven, named Kartashov, and he was sitting near the door. Kolya looked at him with dignified amazement.

The fact was that who had founded Troy had become a secret for the whole school, a secret you could only find out by reading Smaragdov, and nobody had Smaragdov but Kolya. One day, when Kolya had his back turned, Kartashov had quickly opened the Smaragdov that lay among Kolya’s books, and at once hit on the passage about the founding of Troy. That was quite a while ago, but he felt uneasy about it and couldn’t bring himself to announce in public that he too knew who had founded Troy. He was afraid of what might happen, and of Krassotkin somehow shaming him over it. But now he couldn’t help saying it. For weeks he had been longing to.

“Well, who did found it?” asked Kolya, turning to him with haughty superiority. He saw from the boy’s face that he really did know, and he made up his mind at once how to take it. There was, so to speak, a jarring note in the general harmony.

“Troy was founded by Teucer, Dardanus, Ilius and Tros,” the boy rapped out at once, and in the same instant he blushed, blushed so deeply that it hurt to look at him. But the boys stared at him, stared at him for a whole minute, and then all the staring eyes swung round together and fixed on Kolya, who was still looking the bold boy over with scornful calm.
“In what sense did they found it?” he condescended to say at last. “And what does it mean, to found a city or a state? What do they do? Did each of them go and lay a brick, do you suppose?”
There was laughter. The guilty boy went from pink to crimson. He said nothing and was close to tears. Kolya kept him like that for a minute.

“Before you talk about a historical event like the founding of a nation, you must first understand what you mean by it,” he lectured him, in stern, cutting tones. “As for me, I attach no importance to these old wives’ tales, and I don’t think much of universal history in general,” he added carelessly, to the company at large.
“Universal history?” the captain asked, looking almost frightened.

“Yes, universal history! It’s a study of one folly of mankind after another, and nothing more. The only subjects I respect are mathematics and natural science,” said Kolya. He was showing off, and he stole a glance at Alyosha; his was the one opinion he feared there. But Alyosha was still silent and still serious. One word from Alyosha would have stopped him, but Alyosha said nothing, and “it might be the silence of contempt,” and that finally made Kolya angry.
“The classical languages too ... they’re plain madness, nothing else. You seem to disagree with me again, Karamazov?”
“I don’t agree,” said Alyosha, with a faint smile.

“The study of the classics, if you want my opinion, is just a police measure. That’s the only reason it was brought into our schools.” Gradually Kolya was growing breathless again. “They brought in Latin and Greek because they’re a bore and they numb the mind. School was dull already, so what could they do to make it duller? It was senseless enough already, so what could they do to make it more senseless? So they hit on Greek and Latin. That’s my opinion, and I hope I never change it,” Kolya finished abruptly. His cheeks were flushed.
“That’s true,” Smurov agreed suddenly, in a ringing voice of conviction. He had been listening closely.
“And yet he’s first in Latin himself,” one of the boys in the group called out suddenly.
“Yes, father, he says that, and still he’s first in Latin,” Ilusha echoed.

“What of it?” Kolya felt he had to defend himself, though the praise was very sweet to him. “I’m slogging away at Latin because I have to, because I promised my mother I’d pass my examination, and I think that whatever you do, it’s worth doing well. But deep down I have a profound contempt for the classics and all that fraud.... You don’t agree, Karamazov?”
“Why ‘fraud’?” Alyosha smiled again.

“Well, all the classical authors have been translated into every language, so it wasn’t to study the classics that they brought in Latin, but only as a police measure, to numb the intelligence. So what can you call it but a fraud?”
“Why, who taught you all this?” cried Alyosha, surprised at last.
“For one thing, I can think for myself without being taught. And besides, what I just said about the classics being translated, our teacher Kolbasnikov has said to the whole third class.”
“The doctor’s here!” cried Nina, who had said nothing until then.

A carriage belonging to Madame Hohlakov drove up to the gate. The captain, who had been waiting for the doctor all morning, rushed headlong out to meet him. “Mamma” pulled herself together and put on a dignified look. Alyosha went over to Ilusha and began straightening his pillows. From her invalid chair, Nina watched anxiously while he set the bed in order. The boys hurriedly said their goodbyes. Some promised to come back in the evening. Kolya called Perezvon, and the dog jumped down off the bed.
“I’m not going away, I’m not going away,” Kolya said hastily to Ilusha. “I’ll wait in the passage and come back when the doctor’s gone. I’ll come back with Perezvon.”

But by now the doctor had come in, an important-looking man with long dark whiskers and a shiny, clean-shaven chin, wearing a bearskin coat. On the threshold he stopped, taken aback; he probably thought he had come to the wrong place. “What is this? Where am I?” he muttered, taking off neither his coat nor his peaked sealskin cap. The crowd, the poverty of the room, the washing hung on a line in the corner, all puzzled him. The captain, bent double, was bowing low before him.
“It’s here, sir, here, sir,” he muttered, cringing. “It’s here, you’ve come to the right place, you were coming to us...”
“Sne-gi-ryov?” the doctor said loudly and pompously. “Mr. Snegiryov—is that you?”
“That’s me, sir!”
“Ah!”

Once more the doctor gave the room a squeamish look, and threw off his coat, displaying the grand decoration at his neck for all to see. The captain caught the fur coat in mid-air, and the doctor took off his cap.
“Where is the patient?” he asked emphatically.
